newsitem.title: USA: Strain of HPV linked to recurring cervical cancer.
newsitem.headline: Strain of HPV linked to recurring cervical cancer.

text.p: A specific strain of the virus that causes genital warts may be linked to particularly aggressive cases of cervical cancer, scientists said on Tuesday.

If confirmed in larger scale clinical trials, the finding could help doctors determine which women need radiation or other additional therapy after cancer surgery, said Dr. Sharon Wilczynski of the City of Hope National Medical Centre in Duarte, California, and a co-author of the report appearing Wednesday in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute.
Researchers over the past few years have accumulated mounting evidence that the human papilloma virus (HPV), a sexually transmitted virus that causes genital warts, is a factor in cervical cancer.
They have been trying to sort out which strains of the virus are most likely to cause cancer, and, even more specifically, to determine if some strains are responsible for the most dangerous tumours.
The City of Hope team found that HVP type 18 is linked to poor prognosis for cancer, independent of other risk factors such as lymph node involvement and the depth of the tumour invasion.
If detected early by a pap smear, cervical cancer or precancerous cell abnormalities can usually be treated and cured. Still, about 160,000 women worldwide die each year from cervical cancer.
